I pull black mold out of air conditioner drain lines for a living.

In Little Rock, you see every kind of slime imaginable growing inside dark, damp vents.

Yet last September, I found the exact same fungus growing inside my own mouth.

Let me back up.

My name is Travis Caldwell. I am fifty-two years old and I have worked HVAC in Pulaski County for twenty-six years.

My dentist made me a five-hundred-dollar acrylic night guard to stop me grinding my teeth flat.

Every morning, I gave it a quick rinse in the sink and shut it inside its plastic case on the counter.

It sat in that closed, dark box for sixteen hours a day.

By late summer, I was waking up every morning with a raw throat, hacking cough, and heavy sinus pressure.

Two rounds of antibiotics did nothing. The morning cough kept coming back.

Meanwhile, my night guard was turning gross yellow and cloudy.

I scrubbed it with a toothbrush and paste, leaving a cloudy white film.

I bought blue fizzing denture tablets for twenty dollars a month, but the guard still felt slippery and coated.

I even bought a thirty-dollar vibrating cleaner off Amazon. The motor died in three weeks.

My breaking point hit on Interstate 40 when a coughing fit forced me to pull my van onto the shoulder.

That night, I opened the case. The guard smelled like a stagnant drip pan.

The next morning, I showed it to Keith, our senior air quality inspector.

Keith looked at the hinges, shook his head, and told me I was wearing an incubator.

He explained that dental acrylic is full of microscopic pores that soak up moisture like a sponge.

When you shut a wet appliance in a dark case at room temperature, mold spores and Candida yeast multiply rapidly.

Keith said, Think of a wet sponge sealed inside a dark plastic bag. In twelve hours, it stinks of mildew. That is what you press against your gums every night.

Brushing only scratches the acrylic, creating deeper trenches for bacteria and yellow stains to dig in.

Then he told me to test it.

Scrape your thumbnail along the inside ridge where your molars sit.

If a greasy white film comes off, or the case smells like wet drywall, that is live fungal biofilm and bacteria.

I did it that night. My thumbnail scraped up a layer of cloudy slime. It smelled rotten.

Keith told me real cleaning requires four things: forty-two thousand hertz sound waves, medical-grade UV-C light, plain tap water, and a stainless steel basin that cleans in five minutes.

That is when he told me about the DentalPULSE Pod.

Dentists recommend it because it delivers clinical-grade cleaning at home using only tap water. No chemicals, no tablets, no subscription.

I ordered one. When it arrived, I filled the stainless steel tank with plain tap water, dropped my cloudy night guard in, and pushed the button.

After five minutes, the cycle stopped automatically.

The water was murky and brownish-yellow. That was the bacteria, plaque, and trapped gunk leaving my night guard.

My night guard came out crystal clear again, not milky. No white film anywhere.

It stops it turning yellow, and that sour mildew smell was completely gone.

Within ten days, my morning cough stopped. My throat cleared up. The sinus headaches were completely gone.

I still spend my days clearing mold and sludge out of air handlers across Arkansas.

Now, nothing goes into my mouth that is not thoroughly sanitized.
